utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. Before I call for the appearances, I wish to indicate for the record that, again, due to the continued indisposition of Judge Harhoff, we are sitting under the provisions of Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for the Prosecution, Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness comes back in, can I formally apply for more time as I indicated yesterday. Having reviewed what is left yesterday evening and having being told that I have already taken two hours and 50 minutes, which I had not appreciated. I suppose one could it's amazing how time flies when one is enjoying oneself. However, can I ask formally if I may have between an extra hour and 90 minutes, taking it up to a total of five and a half. I hope to complete within 2 hours and 10 minutes, but there is still a lot of documents to be evidenced. And his own account of what happened to him after the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we formally rule on that application that you are now making, we are trying to work backwards, as it were, from the -- what is fixed for Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And bearing in mind the time that is -- would be required for cross-examination and re-examination, I suppose, where do you think that this would place us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm trying -- the Defence estimates for cross-examination were ... four plus one. So that is four hours for Stanisic, one for Zupljanin. That's five hours. Hour and a half -- sorry, an extra hour and a half for me would take us up to just before the second break, I think. Give or take. So that should still leave time for Monday for the Defence to be completed. And obviously if I'm denied my re-examination, I have to accept that's -- that's something that I will have to deal with. But I appreciate we've got videolink lined up for Tuesday through Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It has been confirmed to us that there is a courtroom available on -- on Monday morning, because the -- we were scheduled on Monday afternoon. And is the -- is it premature to think now, in terms of resumption on Monday morning with an extension into the afternoon with a view to finishing this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that would be very helpful if I may so. We all hope that it's completed, if we can sit Monday morning, by Monday morning. And I know that the witness in particular would -- would wish to be completed. Indeed, I understand from VWS he had not appreciated the possibility that he might be here on Monday. And I think maybe we need to do deal with that. But I think certainly we would -- obviously we would have to be completed on Monday, and I think that would help, if it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we grant your application for the extra time, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The Registry will make arrangements for the court to sit the usual morning session on Monday and then one extra session in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if that disposes of preliminary considerations, would the usher kindly escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, Ms. Korner, is the witness aware of the fact that he is expected to be here on Monday as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The answer is, I'm not sure. I think he has realized it because he raised with VWS there was a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One told us that he already had a problem being here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know. And now I understand from VWS he has raised the problem of Monday. Just before the witness comes in, the letter that he received from the home office which was -- reference was simply said he had to report here for Thursday or Wednesday. And it didn't make it clear, although there is a further letter which you may have seen saying he is at the disposal of the Court, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Ms. Korner resumes her examination-in-chief, we should alert you that having been informed that there may have been some miscommunication in the information provided to you, as regards the length of time that you were expected to be before the Tribunal. We should now put you in the picture so that any consequential personal and domestic arrangements as you may have to make, you may do so. It is now anticipated -- it is clear that your testimony would not have been concluded by the time the Court rises today at 1.45, and that you will be required to return on Monday, and it is expected that your testimony would be completed on Monday, and you be released by mid-afternoon on Monday. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, I want to -- I want to start today by continuing the chronological progression, if we can, through 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I reply to His Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand your explanation, and I accept and there is no any question about my co-operation and assistance to this Tribunal. I should remind you and inform you that I received a letter from home office, and that I'm required to testify for 28th of January. In my phone conversation with officials from Tribunal, I accepted possibility to stay on Friday as well. However, I have -- my already booked duties regarding my employment, and regarding duties that I should attend in middle of February in Sydney. I understand, I would say, comfortable decision by Tribunal to finish testimony as soon as possible on one, I would say, part, instead of coming again. And I accept that. I just received a fax letter from home office of UK saying that my further staying here is a matter of the Tribunal. I would appreciate if Tribunal can issue, like, letter or statement to my employer and subject in Sydney saying that I should stay until, of course, decision by Tribunal that I am not necessary to be here anymore. And that my planned duties could be in some state delayed because of my duties to Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and we would be happy to arrange the issue of such a letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, at a document that you saw, I think you have seen before. It's 1809. If we go, for a moment -- well, the second page, it's -- in English not in B/C/S. I think it's all on one page. This is a document that is going out under the name of Mr. Delimustafic. And then if we go back to the first page. Can we just pull up the first page in B/C/S for a moment, because we can see the signature at the bottom, or the name. Yeah. It's addressed - and if we go to the top of the B/C/S, please - to the chief of the CSBs, the SJBs, and to the secretary of the interior. And it's stressing, as the first paragraph says, that the reserve police force must not be used ... engaged in ways and situations that are not stipulated by the law. And then it goes on to point out what the law is, in paragraphs 1, 2, and 3. Now, first of all, I think you were familiar with this document, is that right, at the time it was issued?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question answer on English or my first language?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Yes, this document is known to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you could, sorry, sir, if you could stick to Serbian for the purposes of Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the reason that Mr. Delimustafic sent this document? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delimustafic didn't send this letter or communication to all chiefs of CSBs and the SUP in his own name but on behalf of the collegium. We received instructions or, rather, information that reserve police officers were used in contravention of the instructions and rules of the SUP. At the moment, I cannot be more precise and say how many police stations were involved. There was a misuse to the effect of the restructuring of personnel, especially the executive positions. Then the manning of the reserve police, without prior approval, so we thought that we should inform all the chiefs to take all measures necessary and, in line with the law, to prevent this use or, rather, misuse of the reserve police force. The reserve police force must be used only in accordance with the Law on the Internal Affairs, as set out in the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina, issue 17/19.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think we'll hear from other evidence what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so marked and admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P896, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to go back, please, to some intercepts, again, that you listened to. The first one is a conversation again between you and Mr. Karadzic on the 24th of July. And could we have up, please, 1038.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Madam Korner, if you don't mind -- [Interpretation] I would just like to follow up on your question about item 1 of this communication. We didn't only have operational information about the misuse I spoke about, but some chiefs of SJBs informed us that some commanders of police stations without the approval of the SUP or the Security Service launched some actions of the reserve police that were not in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The tab number of intercept is 17, but I think Dr. Zepinic is still dealing with the last document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what -- can you give us an example, just very briefly, of what these actions were, that were against -- not in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any manning of the reserve police, any personnel change in the reserve police, should have been done in accordance with the law. In some police stations we found out that the manning of the reserve force was going on contrary to the Law on the Internal Affairs. That there was -- the restructuring of personnel and manning of the reserve force, including executives, in contravention of the agreed criteria that set out basic characteristics of the personalities of those who could be reserve police officers. First and foremost that they don't have a criminal record and that they have never been in conflict with the law. Secondly, what was also very important was the fact that the reserve police, in some police stations or, rather, in all police stations, had to, if possible, reflect the ethnic composition of the population of the respective municipality. We had some operational knowledge or information that there had been some tipping of this -- that the national balance or ethnic balance had been tipped in some cases, and some reserve police officers were used for regular activities in some police stations, even though the police stations had the right to call up reserve police only for training but not for active duties without the approval of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can now go back for you, sir, to the intercepts you listened to. It's you and Mr. Karadzic on the 24th of July. And again at the beginning of -- I mean, I think have you listened to this. Could you confirm it is your voice and that of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is some discussion again about arming his escort. And then can we go to the second page, please, in B/C/S and -- sorry, English, and the -- it's still on the first page, no, sorry, and the second page in B/C/S as well. You say to him, we look at the bottom, yes, pull up -- thank you. That you had meetings this morning, and you were visited by or talked to Mico -- Mica. Again, can you tell us who you're talking about there?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that Mica was Mico Stanisic. At this moment, I can't remember any other Mica that I may have spoken to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Karadzic says to you: "Aha, let me tell you, please, this thing about the reorganisation going on, we have to see to see exactly what is the meaning of this reorganisation, and also don't let them remove a single man of yours if you don't want to ..." Can you recall now what reorganisation he was talking about and telling you not to remove a single man?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in keeping with the dispatch that was sent to all security centres and the city SUP, after that, we embarked on a certain personnel shakeup and replenishment of the reserve forces of the police, including recruiting younger and more capable staff. The reorganisation of the reserve staff was probably due to take place a few laters [as interpreted] into our coming to power. Mr. Karadzic's intervention was to say that at all cost we had to respond to some partisan requests as any other party leader, and I respected that. However, there was no direct pressure on us to respond to what party leaders wanted us to do or wanted to implement, not only among the active force but also the reserve force of the Ministry of the Interior. And that was to have party candidates who were loyal to certain political parties instead of being professionals who would carry out their tasks professionally under the Law on Internal Affairs. This is customary pressure being exerted on the part of Dr. Karadzic. He wanted to achieve as much as possible, what the party wanted him to achieve. And that was to have party people in many positions, as many as possible, rather than professionals. In the Ministry of Interior our position was that our members could be party members. They could be members of ethnically-based parties; however, their affiliation to an ethnically-based party could not have had any influence on our request for the tasks to be carried out professionally and in keeping with the law. If the -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you have explained, and I just want to ask you about one other aspect of this conversation. Could you go to the fourth page in English -- could we go to the fourth page in English and the third page in B/C/S. And we can see there at the -- towards the bottom of the page in English Karadzic saying to you: "Don't let go of a single one," talking to Simovic. And you then say to him: "Who shall I get instead of Kezunovic?"

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your pronunciation is quite good.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's unusual. So you were seeking his advice, were you, as to who should become appointed within the police?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that this is a misinterpretation of my question, the one that I put to Dr. Karadzic. This was an instances involving a person who was an engineer communications expert in the Ministry of the Interior, and he was there even before we came into power. He was a very conscious and responsible professional, and I was very surprised that Dr. Simovic as the vice-president of the government had some combination involving Mr. Kezunovic which excluded me or anybody else. I suppose that we should have had previous negotiations about that, and I realized from my conversation with Mr. Karadzic that Mr. Kezunovic was supposed to be transferred to the Ministry of Defence. And in my conversation I told Mr. Karadzic that I didn't agree with that. And that's why I asked him who I should find to replace him, because that person was a very well qualified and experienced engineer. He had spent a lot of time in that position, and leaving a gap in his place meant that there would be -- a gap, it would be impossible to carry out the tasks that Mr. Kezunovic was involved in. I did not agree with that, and my question is actually seeking advice from Dr. Karadzic -- actually, it is not seeking advice from Dr. Karadzic. My question is more a protest against Mr. Karadzic's and Mr. Simovic's initiative to transfer Mr. Kezunovic from his position in the Ministry of Interior to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the point of all of this is that, although Mr. Karadzic had no power to transfer or do anything, he was pretty insistent, from what you -- being said about what should happen, in respect of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say just in respect of Serbs. Political leaders put pressure on all types of appointments. In this particular case, yes, Dr. Karadzic was insisting on a person who was a Serb by ethnicity. However, as far as I remember, Dragan Kezunovic stated that he was in Yugoslav. His father had a been a hero from Romanija, Mr. Stanisic knew him very well, a very well-respected family. So in this case, we're talking just about one candidate, but that was common practice to intervene at all costs in terms of personnel shakeups or personnel appointments. This is one obvious way, as it were, of an unfair relationship between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Simovic. Something that bypassed us from the ministry where Mr. Kezunovic was employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As we will see, because I want to continue with this conversation, Mr. Karadzic was becoming quite emphatic. Can we move please to the next page in English, I think it's still the same page in B/C/S. Karadzic says to you: "Please arrange for the collegium to meet every morning, see what happened the previous day and what's plan for that day. See that no one is appointed without the full approval of all Serbs." And you then intervene and say: "I don't know. I have to consult with Simovic." And Karadzic says: "Because this will result, we've prepared an alternatively which will be atrocious. We prepared it, and we'll fuck their mothers. But to stop that from happening, let them sit every day and for this to --" I mean. Now, when he said, We've prepared an alternative which will be atrocious, you didn't ask him what he was talking about. So what did you understand that he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reply, and I'm sure it will be difficult to translate this conversation and similar conversations with Dr. Karadzic and the other leaders, was just shooting the breeze, nothing else. It was nothing but shooting the breeze. I don't know whether the interpreter has been able to interpret this properly. If not then I will do the interpretation and use the proper reading. So what was -- what was said in those conversations had nothing whatsoever to do with the reality of the matter, and I find -- found it surprising that political leaders were still not able to understand that they did not have any right to influence the appointment of the personnel the way that they thought they could. When it comes to some alternatives, cursing, swear words, and these language inappropriate -- in a civilised word, I can say nothing else but this was just shooting the breeze. That should not have been understood seriously. It did not mandate any further discussion. Nothing serious would have arisen from that anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But the question, sorry, Dr. Zepinic was this. He says we have prepared an alternative which will be atrocious. We have prepared it, and we'll fuck their mothers. Now you didn't ask him what he was talking about, so whether you took it seriously or not, what did you understand his threat to mean?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you had an occasion, and I'm sure you did, to look at all the other conversations, the customary tone or language that Dr. Karadzic used, and I'm not going be repeating the terms that he was using in the conversations, and to be honest, I don't know who he meant. He is using a swear word and somebody's mother, I don't know whose. Mine? Yours? Muslim's mother? Croatian's mother? Mr. Stanisic's mother? It is just talking stupidities that I did not even give a second thought to. I did not want to go into further discussions as to who he was threatening, how he was threatening to do whatever he wanted -- was going to do. We didn't -- not have any clear evidence as whom he was threatening, and then we would have reported him for that. But we didn't have that. This was just his customary way of saying next to nothing in a very stupid way, and it really did not call for any other discussions or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's look, shall we, and maybe we can get some enlightenment what he was saying to you later on. Page 9 in the English, please. And --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I'm not smoking. I am coughing. I understand you, Madam, but I don't know what is going on with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm afraid it is catching. Can we have look at page 9 in the English and -- the page numbers don't seem to be marked in the B/C/S, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, in the B/C/S. Yeah. Now in the middle of the page in B/C/S near the top in this. Mr. Karadzic says to you, continuing with the theme: "Please let the collegium meet every morning and clear all that out. I was with Izetbegovic last night and with Zulfikarpasic, and I told him right into his face, We'll establish a parallel government, parallel police, or withdraw our people, and they'd have to be paid by the government. Withdraw all our people under arms. We'll then establish an entire parallel state if you keep on screwing us. "And he just looked and blinked because we'll do that. Not even God could stop us in that, because they started to fuck with us and to fuck us up, and there is no doubt we will do all of that in a week. So let there be war, let there be war, but we'll finish the job for once." And your response to that was: "At least we'll know where we are." Now, when you heard this, this was a plain, plain threat, wasn't it, about setting up a parallel government in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree it is leading. But, all right, if you can find any other way of describing it, Mr. Krgovic, I will happily take your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you heard this, did you -- why didn't you say something about it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please remind me of the date of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. It's July -- 24th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. 24th July 1991, nothing happened for the following next -- for the following seven days despite what Dr. Karadzic said. And my comment was, Okay, we -- we will know where we stand, hoping and looking forward to Mr. Karadzic and other leaders doing what they promised to do. We should have only been so lucky if they had -- the coalition would have broken down. There would be no more ethnically-based parties. There should have been new elections and ethnically-based parties would not have won. If I could influence Dr. Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and Kljuc, and make them do what he promised he would, I would be very happy because there would probably be no war in my country. I had an meeting in Zulfikarpasic and Alija Izetbegovic, and in all the conversations, it is mentioned that they had met. Whether they did or not, it's up to them. In any case I cannot accept the fact that what Dr. Karadzic said to Zulfikarpasic or Izetbegovic that Mr. Izetbegovic as the president of the Presidency or the president of the SDA, did not react to any of that, because it -- if it was an open threat that means that there was no coalition, that there was no partnership in power. My comment was, at least we will know where we stand, and what this meant was that I really wanted to know what political and ethnically-based parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina were up to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But the real question is, your response is at least we will know where we are. Was there any reason why you didn't say to him words to the effect of, Don't be stupid. That is not going to get us anywhere; that is going to lead us to war?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to say that in official meetings, in government sessions, Presidency session, and assembly sessions. Not once. I'm sure I will not exaggerate if I say that that I was really adamant in telling them that ethnically-based parties are not good for Bosnia-Herzegovina but that, rather, their political agendas can only lead to a crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In an interview where I was attacked, I said that a war would bring at least 100.000 dead and 2 million people who have move from their homes. I was even too optimistic when I mentioned the figure of 100.000 according to the current data that 250.000 people eventually died. Did say that at official meetings of a various institutions and at my meetings with the leaders. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I absolutely accept that, Dr. Zepinic. I'm just asking why, given that you said this on television and at meetings, why you didn't say that in this private conversation with Dr. Karadzic. That's all.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In private conversations that we had, given the tone and the structure of this particular conversation that he had had with Mr. Zulfikarpasic, Izetbegovic, and the threats, in a private conversation I could do you know what. Let me not tell you what it would have been. Because this is just not my style, and that's why I did not use the lingo that involved swear words that Mr. Karadzic so freely used in -- in his conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then, finally, on this conversation, could we go to page 10 in English, and to - sorry, I have to count out the pages - 7 in B/C/S. At the bottom -- I'm sorry. You say to Dr. Karadzic that, Mico will see you in the morning at 8.30. And he says, Stanisic. And you say, Yes, and we'll discuss that, and I'll let you know what we did. Now, did you have meetings with Mico Stanisic to discuss the appointment or replacement of personnel?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic had been appointed as secretary of the Sarajevo SUP and general region which included territory of Romanija, and when it came to personnel issues, I talked to all the chiefs, including Mr. Stanisic. It was only natural that the selection of personnel was to the satisfaction of the chief of the security services centre, rather than those candidates being imposed by the ministry. We wanted to find the best possible joint solution for a person that would be working as a team member together with Mr. Stanisic. Therefore, I suppose that we did have a meeting to discuss personnel issues. My initiative was to sit down with everybody over a cup of coffee irrespective of the pressures of political parties. It was only natural and customary when it came to appointments of lower-ranking personnel or command personnel in the police stations or security centres to have a word with the respective chiefs, including the Sarajevo SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this conversation was about, in fact, I don't want to go back to it, the Deputy Chief for Defence Preparations and the State Security Service, wasn't it? And Devedlaka's appointments.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not stated precisely whether that was the matter at hand. However, within the Sarajevo SUP, there was also the Department of State Security and Mr. Stanisic, as the chief of the security services centre in Sarajevo was responsible for the functioning of the State Security Service for the Sarajevo region. And that applied to any other chief who had a state security department within the -- their respective security services centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. From your observation of Mico Stanisic and Dr. Karadzic, what did you gain the impression, was their relationship? In other words, was it a close relationship, a distant one?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their closeness or lack of closeness, their friendship, was their private matter. I was not interested in that. What I was interested in was to what extent Mr. Stanisic was capable of performing his tasks without caving in to pressures, including pressures from Dr. Karadzic. And irrespective of the possible relationship that existed between the two of them. My observation, with regard to their relationship is absolutely irrelevant. I was never interested in that. I did not pay any attention to that, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I -- Dr. Zepinic, this was a question you were asked in the statement you made. Do you remember that? Whether you think it's irrelevant, that's what you were asked. Do you remember making a statement about this?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I provided a lot of statements. I can only say that, yes, they had a quite a close relationship. I don't know whether it was friendship and what was the base of their relationship. That was not up to me to -- to say or pay attention to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, but I'm just asking for your observation, that's all. And your observation is -- is that they had quite a close relationship, but you can't say if it was friendship. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, when it comes to interpretation, we have to bear in mind, and I am kindly asking the interpreter to allow me to explain that. In Bosnia and Herzegovina a relationship among people fell into four categories. He's my colleague, my work colleague, my friend, or an acquaintance. In English all that would be friend. So the use of any term that falls into the category of friend is probably going to be interpreted in English as friend, although I am using three or four different words in my language. When it comes to English the relationship between myself and Mr. Stanisic or me and Mr. Karadzic is also going to be interpreted as friendship. Unfortunately, we have to make a certain distinction here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see -- when you attended meetings of the SDS, was Mico Stanisic also at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he attended some. I remember that. And he didn't attend others. The first time I was invited to a meeting of the SDS concerning some security issues involving my ministry, I was surprised to see Mr. Stanisic there. And I asked him in what capacity was he present, since the security issues were not on the agenda. At least not the security of the Sarajevo region. If that had been a meeting of the city committee of the SDS, Mico Stanisic would have been duty-bound to attend such a meeting and discuss security issues. However, this was a meeting at the national level, and when I asked him, he replied that he was a party member and that was his own thing, whether he was or not. So I did see him at the party meetings. I can't tell you that it was every time. I can't tell you how many times I saw him. I did not keep track of that. It would have been beyond me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that intercept be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D897, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we next have the intercept - which is at tab 18 of for the interpreters - 1799. It is the same day as the last conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not one to which you were a party, Dr. Zepinic, but you listened to it, and there's a reference to you. Right, this is a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Devedlaka. Firstly, did you know Devedlaka?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us very briefly what his position was at this period in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. If he had been in an important position or played an important role, I would probably remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Which branch of the MUP was he in? Can you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he worked at the centre of the State Security Service of the city SUP. Later, he -- he was a candidate for post in the defence preparations unit or some other unit under Mr. Kresic. But I don't really remember his role in mid-1991, nor what he did, probably because he wasn't in a high position. I remember him well from the time after the war began, when he harassed me and arrested me, but that was later. But while I was in power, I really don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to digress for a small moment from this, but when you listened to this conversation, were you able to recognise his voice and that of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to digress for one moment because I think it's the second time we've dealt with -- or we've mentioned the defence preparation. Could you just explain very briefly to the Court what defence preparation was, or what -- what the defence preparation unit was.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to be more precise in your question. You mean different preparation within my ministry, the CSB, or generally the preparation of defence in the republic? I'm sorry, I don't want to appear as splitting hairs, but I don't want to provide a wrong answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm very grateful. You're quite right, Dr. Zepinic, we should be precise about this. Can we start with what the defence preparation unit within the ministry was. Again, if we could keep this brief because of the time, that would help.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief as possible in my inclination [as interpreted]. As any other ministry, the MUP, too, had a section of defence preparation which drafted plans for the protection of vital facilities in case of crisis or imminent threat of war. These plans also included the engagement of personnel, the SJBs, and the reserve forces of the police in accordance with the need. Likewise, the engagement of the police special forces. Defence preparation also included the drafting of plans with detailed instructions about what any subject in the -- from the SUP to the last police station in the field was supposed -- and obliged to do in case of crisis or imminent threat of war. Defence -- the Department of Defence preparation was duty-bound to make a -- to space, to specify, which equipment was required. When I say "equipment," I mean weapons, protective equipment, gas masks, uniforms, et cetera, anything that can enable the ministry, in case of crisis or imminent threat of war, to function, to be ready and have appropriate plans and equipment to live up to its duties, the duties of the MUP, under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That's -- now, first -- sorry, first thing arising from that is, you said it had plans -- it drew up plans for the engagement of the police special forces. Was it in any way connected with the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The defence preparation unit. In other words, did it come under the command --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Under which --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the special unit was under the exclusive command, as I explained yesterday, of Delimustafic and me. And within the special unit there was a person who drew up plans and specified the equipment required for the special unit and forwarded that to the sector of defence preparation of the MUP to organise supply. So the defence preparation was the executive part of the overall planning and preparation activities but not in the position to issue any orders or indeed a request to any unit to go into action to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And within the ministry, before we come to the CSBs, the defence preparation unit -- or department, was that a separate department, or did each department within the ministry have somebody tasked with that function?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Defence preparations within the MUP were not a separate department or unit, and the same applies to the CSB. In the centre of State Security Service, there was also a defence preparation unit that took care of equipping or specifying equipment for the requirements of the State Security Service, including surveillance, wire-tapping and whatever state security is supposed to do. I don't need to elaborate. But, essentially the defence preparation unit in no service, be it the CSB or the state security, was a -- was an autonomous service and couldn't function as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. So within the CSBs, was it, as you described, that each of the departments we've seen would have somebody tasked with defence preparation?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the CSB there would be a unit or a single officer, depending on the size of the respective CSB. The largest CSBs were those in Banja Luka and Sarajevo, so I suppose that there were more than one staff in that unit. And in others there was only one who was in charge of issuing equipment and taking care of the quantities of weapons and other equipment available to enable the CSB to function properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry, we digressed. So can we go back to this intercept. And if we go to the second page in the English, and it's still on the first page in the B/C/S. To put this in context, Karadzic is asking Devedlaka, and this is the same day you had spoken to Karadzic, about his nomination of somebody from Romanija. And Devedlaka denies it. And then Karadzic says to him, Please call Zepinic now, because he told me that you had proposed this man. No one has the right to put forward personal proposals. You have staff meetings, everyone's voice should be heard? Devedlaka replies, I went to his office this morning and told him I did not support this man Suka because he is incompetent. And then Karadzic says, Why has Vito nominated him? And Devedlaka says, I don't know. Had there been a conversation between you and Devedlaka to the -- to the effect of what he told Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I cannot remember a conversation about the appointment of Mr. Suka. I really don't remember. The comment of Dr. Karadzic is a bit strange, when he says, Well, why does Vito propose him? Whether I proposed him or Mr. Stanisic and whether that had to do with the CSB of Sarajevo, I really cannot say. Whether I spoke to Devedlaka, probably in passing. But whether there was a decision on my part about the appointment of Suka, I really don't know. I don't even remember who that guy Suka was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that just be marked for identification then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P898, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to, please, to document 1044, and it's tab 22 for the interpreters. It is an intercept again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this appears to be, in fact, as we will see, a three-way conversation on the 2nd of September of 1991. Mr. Karadzic, yourself, and we'll see later somebody called Rajko is also present. Now have you listened to this conversation. Were you able to identify your voice and that of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the man Rajko who apparently -- can you hear him when you listen to the conversation, or not?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot confirm that, because I really don't remember. I have listened to so many conversations. I can't remember each and every one. So I can't give an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's just start at the beginning, very quickly on this one. At the bottom of page 1 in the English. And somewhere in the middle, not quite at the bottom. Karadzic says to you: "Vito, have I been trying to reach you, but could I not get through. People from Vogosca are with me. There will be barricades and all sort of things there." This is September 1991. Can you recall why there were going to be barricades in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of the MUP, or, rather, at the MUP we had no such information. As far as I know, and Mr. Stanisic will know better, because that was within the CSB Sarajevo, there weren't any barricades eventually. But that was the usual style of exerting pressure on the part of Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Izetbegovic and so on. If you do not give in to our demands, then we will raise 10.000 people. We will take weapons, and this and that. But I never took that seriously. This is probably about some personnel issues at the CSB or the police station of Vogosca. I cannot give you a specific answer now, but if I can take a look at the -- at how the conversation continues, then I may be. But this thing about the barricades was a bluff, which was -- which we were faced with daily. These were threats that were not addressed only to my ministry. There were also threats to me personally or to my family. But that was, as it were, the normal style of the people I was confronted with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We can see the next -- in fact, the next part in English, and I think it is already on the B/C/S, explains that this is -- the barricades are going to be raised because of an appointment. Because you asked why. Now, I want to move, please, to the fourth page in English, and it's the third page, I think, in B/C/S. You ask at the top of -- I'm not -- yes, we have the right one. "Dr. Karadzic, do we have a chief of the town SUP?" And Mr. Karadzic says: "The chief of the SUP says that the MUP is going to make appointments later on. We can ... give me an answer straight away because I want to clarify this. Is he or not? Can he write a letter of appointment and appoint a man?" You say: "Who?" And he says: "Chief of the town SUP." Question: "Why didn't he make a proposal?" Karadzic: "Wait a second. Why didn't he make it ... you are, please, have you been warned in the MUP that this man cannot be appointed." And you say: "By whom?" And you say: "By the municipality?" Karadzic says: "By the municipality, by the Executive Committee." Now, was the Executive Committee issue warnings to the MUP about appointments?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this conversation, it is it obvious that Dr. Karadzic didn't have the faintest idea about the functioning or about how people were appointed. First and foremost, it was normal to consult the secretary of the SUP of the town in question. If we consider the date of this conversation, then we know that it is Mr. Stanisic. Dr. Karadzic is confusing apples and pears here. The town -- the City Committee and the Executive Committee of the municipality are two separate bodies. The Executive Committee of the town had no interest in the appointment of a commander of a police station in Vogosca. So these comments of his are nonsensical. That is why I had trouble understanding him, because obviously he was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to just continue very quickly to finish this conversation before the break. The -- as I say, the -- Rajko, who is in the room, has a conversation there with Karadzic. Can we go to the next page in English, 5. And whoever it is says: "I went to see Zepinic. I called him personally in Dudjaskovic [sic]." And he says: "Then I went to see Zepinic two months ago --" Go over the page in the English to the next page. And it's -- in the B/C/S, it's the fourth page, fourth page in B/C/S. This Rajko is saying: "I called Mandic," and then he says, "what did Mandic say?" "It will not happen. He called Draskovic ... he called Stanisic, but Stanisic was the only one who said he is helpless and he cannot control anything." And you were asked: "Did you hear this?" And you say: Yes, I heard everything." Now, does that remind you of who the Rajko was? Very quickly, if it doesn't, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this is Rajko Dukic because he was the chairman of the executive board of the Serbian Democratic Party, and it was his duty in the party to take care of personnel issues at the level of BiH. I think it was Mariofil Ljubic for the Croats, and Muhammed Cengic for the SDA, who were in the same positions, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation that took place here -- [In English] Can I continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just going to ask -- Yes, can I just before you continue --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- Dr. Karadzic -- you say you heard everything. Karadzic says, Stanisic says he cannot control anything because is he not writing letters of appointment; they're coming from the MUP. You say, Dr. Karadzic, if he is helpless, he should resign. And Karadzic says, Come on, we must check who else is helpless and who else has to resigned, because Stanisic is not the only one. I have to deal with the crap that is going to cause a civil war. Now, tell us, please, yes, about this conversation. Stanisic saying that he could not control anything and Karadzic agreeing, was that an accurate portrayal of Mico Stanisic's position?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of conversation went on between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Stanisic, I don't know. And about Mr. Karadzic's remark that Stanisic is helpless, this isn't the first time I say that. If any chief of a CSB feels helpless and unable to do anything, then it would be fair to resign. And that applied to me too. It is true that Mr. Stanisic could not decide on the appointment of anyone, not even a police constable in any police station of the Sarajevo CSB without a decision from the ministry. Mr. Stanisic, like any other chief of a CSB, was consulted about executive positions because a team to had to be established that could function. But, the minister or his deputy or any assistant in the MUP could not check or verify what -- the chief of the CSB about the appointment of a police officer. That was within -- within somebody else's remit and Mr. Stanisic, like any other chief, I repeat, was not in the position to decide about anybody's appointment. That was the job of the personnel service of the MUP. And if Dr. Karadzic, if he were to give in to Dr. Karadzic's insisting, as we can see here, then that would have been a breach of regulation, and he could be held responsible for acting illegally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And one last question --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, think I think the time for the break, but I have just got one last question on this. Yeah. Can we go, in English, please, to page 1821, and in the B/C/S, I am afraid I don't know. I don't think it matters. I just want to -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's just this. Karadzic in the middle of the page allegations that Selimovic has been preparing a civil war, and you're not preventing that. And you say you don't anticipate that. And he says, I'm going to ask Mr. Izetbegovic tomorrow to dissolve the MUP. And you say, I have nothing against that. Did you take that seriously?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I was all for Mr. Izetbegovic and Dr. Karadzic to take a final decision about division, that the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina be saved from the misfortune that the ethnic parties brought upon them. And this about the dissolution of the MUP is nonsense because neither Karadzic nor Izetbegovic were the owners of the MUP. It wasn't their private backyard where they could do what they wanted to. There was a law in force, but, obviously, neither Dr. Karadzic nor Mr. Izetbegovic adhered to its provisions. To their minds, they were the law, and they could do what they want because they were in power.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P899, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we take the break at this point. We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, I'm afraid that my time is rapidly getting shorter. So if we could go fairly swiftly through a few more intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please -- sorry. Now I've got my own notes saying "swiftly." I'm sorry, could we have up document 1803, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this -- last conversation we looked at with you and Dr. Karadzic was the 2nd of September. This is an article in "Oslobodjenje" on the 7th of September of 1991. And it's entitled: The MUP response to Dr. Radovan Karadzic's statement. Now, it appears that there was a press conference of the SDS, and he was complaining publicly, effectively, what we've seen him complain about in these various telephone conversations, and the MUP, apparently, gave a response. Now, did you see this article at the time?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. There was a lot of news reports and other material that we had at the time. My head of office and -- certain services made a short list for me. However, in this document, we pointed out, again, as I had already said on many occasions at some meetings and press conferences that I personally held, that ethnically-based parties were not pursuing policies that led to the stabilisation and progress in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, rather, they led to the state of disintegration and the break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina which inevitably further on led to an armed conflict or war. This is just one of the statements that Mr. Karadzic gave to the press, in which he displayed his displeasure with the work of the Ministry of Interior. The hard-liners of the Ministry of Interior were proposed to be held in the ministry as an organ that carried out its duties in keeping with the law. This is nothing new. This is something that we faced daily in the Ministry of Interior. There are all sorts of attacks and pressures put by political leaders or institutions, if can I call a party an institution. So this would have been our customary reaction to the normal pressures that were put on us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the statement put out by the MUP that: They were untrue, malicious, and calculated to divide the ethnic groups in our Republic, was that something that you believed?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never believed, I never accepted, I still do not accept that the resolution to the post-communist Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was war, and that the only solution for us was to fight and do whatever we had done to us, and to set the country back by at least 50 years, thwarting progress for the next 50 years. War, as a solution, was not a solution, in my mind, because every war has to end up in negotiations. My motto, and I'm sure you will find it in documents, that it is better to negotiate for five years than to wage war for five years. What you see in Dr. Karadzic's interview in which he calls us a new armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm very sorry that we were not better equipped and sooner in order to prevent war. We should have even raised in -- up in arms against anybody who wanted to pursue the war. We were not duty-bound do tell Dr. Karadzic where our arms were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Can I -- can I -- because as I say, I'm sorry about this. I know you have a lot to tell us, but all I'm concerned about in this particular article was these statements put out by the MUP in response to Dr. Karadzic. Were you in agreement with those statements?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the media?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I'm looking at now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] It's no question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P900.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I would like to back please very, very swiftly to intercepts. First of all -- sorry, I just need to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have up 65 ter 10248. And it's divider 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, it's a conversation between you and Dr. Karadzic. This time, on the 9th of September. If you go to the first page, bottom of the page, please. You're saying -- you're telling Dr. Karadzic about gatherings. And Karadzic is, Again, we're talking about blocking Sarajevo. And then second page in English and in B/C/S, please. Again, Dr. Karadzic repeating the threat of barricades. And then him saying in the middle of the English page: "They'll not escape the MUP, our MUP in Krajina, and not only in Krajina but all over Bosnia and Herzegovina ... we shall establish our authority," et cetera. So again, Dr. Zepinic, is it right -- and I appreciate what you say about how you took his threats. He is making more threats of barricades and establishing their own authority. Is that right? If can you just answer yes or no, so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P901.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Moving then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I was distracted momentarily by doing the arithmetical calculation of how much time you have left. And it's an hour and 27 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm very grateful, Your Honours. Even so, there's still a lot to get through. Could we have up, please, on the screen, the next intercept which is 1046. Tab 25, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I think you -- you listened to this and identified your voice that of Dr. Karadzic. If we look at the bottom of the English, yes, Dr. Karadzic is off again, about this time the replacement of a gentleman named Nedjo Vlaski. Very quickly, can you just tell the Court who Mr. Vlaski was.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Vlaski more as being the idiot when I was arrested and how he behaved towards me and my family. He a minor role to play in the State Security Service before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then we see, if we go into the English, in page 2, and I think the B/C/S in page 2 as well. You offer to resign at that stage. And can you just - and I apologise for asking you - could you briefly say why, at this stage, you were offering to resign.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was my second or third attempt at offering my resignation to the government and the Presidency. I had realized that my concept and my political views and thinking, as well as the way I managed the Ministry of Interior, were all in conflict with the policies and intentions of the ethnically-based parties which were then in power. Therefore, I was part of the executive power. I was a member of that executive power, and in any case, I am really surprised that I had not been removed even before, because there was no segment in which I subscribed to the policies of the coalition powers the way they wanted me to do. My resignation was open at any time, but it was never accepted. On two occasions Mr. Krajisnik told me that that resignation could not be made public before the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know why that was impossible, but it is true that I offered my resignation, not once, but on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P902.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you now -- could we have up on the screen, please, 3074. Divider 26 for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not a conversation in which you were involved, but you are referred to, and I just want it ask you about it. Again, this is 17th of September. This is a conversation between Karadzic and Miodrag Simovic who you have referred to on a number of occasions. When you listened to the conversation, were you able to identify the voices?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I identified Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, Dr. Karadzic is saying here that Simovic should tell you - this is in the middle of the page - that, All the ministers and the officials in the MUP will be withdrawn, discontinuing the partnership because you are allowing maltreatment and removal from office. Vlaski removed. Going to break up with Izetbegovic. Establish our own SUP. And then Karadzic says that he should resign immediately -- you, sorry, you should resign immediately if you're able to protect [indiscernible]. And it says you should submit it. Now, did Mr. Simovic speak to you about Karadzic saying you should resign?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that Simovic spoke to me about that. But let me just side track a little. Dr. Simovic was the vice-president of government in charge of internal affairs and political affairs. I don't remember that we discussed that. As far as my resignation is concerned, I have tabled it already in the previous intercept. That resignation was on at all times, and it was available to anyone who wanted it. When it says we will meet again, Izetbegovic and I, I would say that this is it just a customary threat about Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Izetbegovic being able to find a way to break up the MUP. But that's their business, and I -- never occurred to me to pay attention to that. We should only have been so lucky for them to have made and implemented such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that just be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P903, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally for this period of time, can we look at 1048. Divider 27 for the interpreters. This is a conversation between you and Mr. Karadzic, 18th of September, so the day after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have the 65 ter number, I'm sorry. It wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1048. Divider 27. Can we go -- again, I think you listened to this, identified your respective voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go in the English, please, to page 3. And in the B/C/S, it's page 2. And can we move up the English slightly, and the B/C/S too. It's the last -- yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Karadzic, again talking personnel issues, it would appear. And he says to you: "Everything regarding personnel, all these matters should be fixed and finished. This is something I want rectified. Our people have been constantly alert and make sure they don't let them fuck up things in any way. It is down to you as a master of the house to play a crucial role. You're a Serbian minister, and everything that the Serbian people have entrusted to the authorities, they have accordingly entrusted to you and the people who have assembled there." Did you regard yourself as a Serbian minister, in the sense of being answerable to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was accountable and answerable to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Political leaders or parties in power as political parties received information from us, and we participated in their meetings when matters within our purview were discussed, within the purview of our ministry. Not a single party leader under the law, the practice was a different matter, but under the law, no single party leader had the right to intervene in the matters of the Ministry of the Interior, be it in the matter of its functioning, be it in the personnel matters. That is why the political parties had agreed to have three committees that were supposed to meet and possibly propose or table their proposals for the personnel and other relevant facts that were necessary, not only for the functioning of my ministry but also of other ministries. Individual invitations by political leaders were primarily, in my mind, a certain level of pressure that was put on us who were working there. However, we were answerable only to the government, the Presidency, and the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and not to political -- to the political parties. And let me just say that the assembly appointed people as members of government, not as party members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P904.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you now have a look, please, at a document which is exhibit 1805 -- 65 ter number 1805. This is a letter of complaint from the SDA, dated the 8th of October, addressed to Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Delimustafic, and then the third person is you. And it's largely a complaint about the behaviour of Mr. Mandic. Did you receive this document?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I saw this document or not. I can say that, together with Mr. Cengic and Mr. Brko, who was the secretary of the SDA, we held several meetings about personnel issues and the selection of personnel to be put forward by the SDA. I must say that they were satisfied with my positions, just as Mr. Karadzic and others were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just concerned about one aspect of this. One of the complaints -- let me go back to -- it's at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the paragraph which is near the bottom. So if we can move the document up in English. I don't think it's on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They complain that Mandic has managed to give employment to a significant number of his relatives, friends, and family members, including his brother and kum, which I think - I don't understand what that means - Mico Stanisic. Firstly -- was -- did you know whether or not Mico Stanisic was the -- the kum to Momcilo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. In any case, Mr. Stanisic was not appointed the secretary of the Sarajevo SUP because he was Momcilo Mandic's kum. As for the younger Mandic, Momcilo Mandic's brother, he was at the school of the interior, at the time when I was the chief administrative officer of that school. As for the people who Mr. Cengic mentions here, I knew some of them and with great satisfaction, I can say that I kept Vahid Pasic, Idriz Pesic, and Pajnovic, because they were professionals. I am surprised that Mr. Cengic given, on behalf of the SDA, asks why a place couldn't be found for Sredoje Novic or - just a moment, the brain's gone - and Momo Andzic, I believe. They were both Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me. I'm just looking translation here. Firstly, Mico Stanisic was the kum to Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It says Milan Martic, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think that can be right. Line -- sorry, I can't see it on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eighteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be Mandic, not Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, may I ask that this document then be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P905.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, could you have a look, please, at a document that's already been exhibited, very quickly, P180.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise has the counsel just been tendering 1805?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It has already been exhibited as Exhibit P904.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you. Didn't realize that. In which case could I -- P180, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the gazette. And we're moving now really to the end of the year and after there has been the split in the assembly. This is the Ministerial Council of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You are shown as the second person on that council, with Mico Stanisic. We have go down a bit on the page, in English, as number 18. Now, why did you agree to go on to the ministerial council that had been set up by the Assembly of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not on the initiative by the SDS. It was an agreement between the three parties to establish councils or committees of those in power on behalf of the parties. I told you that I had information that the minister of the SDS and the SDA were meeting. This was an initiative on the part of the political parties to establish committees or councils composed of people who acted on behalf of their parties in the positions to which they were appointed by their parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Shall we step back for a moment, please. Stop there, Dr. Zepinic. In October of 1991, the Serbs left the assembly. There had been the passing of the resolution, and I don't want to enter into the legality of that, but the Serbs were establishing -- had established their own assembly. Now, whether or not, as you say, the only other assembly, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly had established a ministerial council, what I'm asking is why you agreed to join a specifically Serb ministerial council.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was in a position that belonged to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know why Mico Stanisic was also put onto the council?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell. Probably because -- but I'm not sure whether he was still secretary of the SUP of Sarajevo at the time, or whether he had been appointed counsellor in the minister's office. Some of the names mentioned here are the names of people I've never met, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And just to complete this, you did actually attend - and I don't think that we need to put up the documents because they're already exhibited - meetings of this ministerial council, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I attended one meeting of this council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think -- I think we'll find it's two. But if we look, please -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe two, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did you understand was the purpose of this Ministerial Council of the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I had expected that the appointment of a council composed of persons who were in certain positions to which they were appointed by their parties, would prove a way of finding agreement among political parties. But my expectations were proven wrong. I believe that you're in possession of documents that show that I didn't participate in the activities of this council, once I understood that it was set up to no avail. These ministerial councils were eventually dissolved. Whether new ones were established later, I don't know. But I'm referring now to the ministerial council whose composition is shown here, and my name figures among the members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you have -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, 45, 3, I believe the witness said that these ministerial councils were eventually dissolved on all three sides. Maybe you can verify that with the witness, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that yesterday documents were shown to me, which say that the Serbian Democratic Party dissolved this ministerial council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's be clear about this, please, Dr. Zepinic. The documents you saw yesterday related to SDS meetings and whatever SDA party meetings. This is alleged to be a ministerial council. What ministerial council existed in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was still meeting during this period?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministerial council was not in existence, as such, when that would have been appointed by the cabinet or the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are ministerial councils appointed by political parties, and they are composed of candidates that held positions in the assembly and the cabinet. And the positions were those that belonged to the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Had, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at that stage, the Croats taken themselves out of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and set up a separate assembly with a ministerial council?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is an misunderstanding, at least judging by your question. The Serbian Democratic Party, the SDA, and the HDZ had their respective assemblies, and they had their bodies, political bodies. And the same parties established their ministerial councils, according to the agreement struck by political leaders, the same way the SDS did as we see in this document. The Croatian Democratic Union, that is the Croats, as far as I know, did not walk out of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and -- [Previous translation continues] [In English] ... Your Honour, if you don't mind, take a little bit time to explain a little bit more about consequences of [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't -- for the moment don't trouble about that. I think we need to establish what we're all talking about here. The Serbs had walked out of the assembly in October 1991. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In -- they had set up their own separate assembly of the SDS, which was separate from the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party, the HDZ and the SDA had existed even before the new government was established. They had their assemblies all the time, and based on that, they nominated their cadres. A new Assembly of the Serbian people or the SDS was not established after the Serbs had walked out of the assembly, but the existing assembly had only continued to function.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you -- all right. You are equating, are you, this -- the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina with party congresses - let's get the terms quite clear, please - or party structures, you are saying this is the same thing. That was your view. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No new candidate was elected, as far as I know, to the Assembly of the SDS once the Serbs had left the coalition partnership in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on then, because, as I say, time is running out. Can we turn now, please, to -- yes, I just want to ask you to look very briefly at the head of this document. It has already been exhibited as P -- no, for some reason, it appears to be a Defence exhibit, which is 1D135, I don't know why, but let's hope it's the right one.
