On the 11th of February 1992, a large gathering of senior police officers was held in Banja Luka. Were you ever told about this gathering at the time, or invited to attend?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't invited, nor did I know about that gathering. But it wasn't their duty to inform me either because I had officially resigned and the Speaker of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina Mr. Krajisnik, accepted my resignation. It was dated the 4th February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that was seven days before this gathering. If they had invited me, I most certainly would not have gone, but I was not invited, nor did they consult me about anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you have made a slight mistake about your resignation because we're going to come to that. You resigned in April, not February. Or rather --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, you're right. Correct. But I was not aware of that gathering, nor was I invited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So neither Mico Stanisic nor Momcilo Mandic told you that this meeting was going to be held or had been held?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Next, can we look at, please -- you asked about Mico Stanisic's appointment. The document is 2596. He was apparently appointed to the -- as an advisor to the State Security Service on the 14th of February, 1992, which is after the appointment of the Council of Ministers. So in your view, as he hadn't been appointed to the position which he held then, was there any reason for him to have been on the Council of Ministers, as a result of him being secretary to the SUP in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was secretary to the SUP in Sarajevo, there may have been a reason for him to be a member of the council, or whatever they called it, because his position was that of a member of the minister's office. And about his appointment as advisor, I don't know about that. I believe Delimustafic signed this. It seems so. So I cannot comment. But there was some disagreement about the carrying out of duties of the secretary to the SUP at Sarajevo, and that probably brought about the replacement of Mico Stanisic and his being appointed advisor at the minister's office. But, as far as I know, his -- his own office was not at the ministry, but he still had his desk, his workplace, at the city SUP, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Are you saying that Mr. Delimustafic didn't discuss with you at all the appointment of Stanisic to this position?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I'm saying that there was some disagreement between the ministry, or, more specifically, me and Mr. Stanisic, because the concept of leadership of the secretary to the SUP of Sarajevo did not match my concept or the concept of the ministry. So that's why any agreement with Mr. Stanisic, decided to appoint him advisor, and I believe that Kemo Sabovic was reinstated in his position because he had been in that position before Mr. Stanisic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P906; and page 43, line 1 through 4 should be Exhibit P905.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I now want to move, please, to the events of the barricades at the beginning of March about which you told us a little yesterday. Can you just tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a correction. It was in early March, not May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I note that the transcript is not precise what the witness has said. I heard the witness say that this -- this change was because of the differences in concept, In agreement with Mr. Stanisic, it was decided to appoint him advisor, and I believe that Kemo Sabovic was reinstated after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says so that's why any agreement then, I don't know, assign with Mr. Stanisic decided to appoint him advisor, so ... I'm not -- I just wanted to be -- to have it precise, if it is possible, please. So maybe the witness can repeat his answer slowly so it can be recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, sir, because we have still got a lot to cover, what did you say about Mr. Stanisic's appointment? Was that with his agreement or with Delimustafic's agreement?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once more and try to be brief and precise. There was open disagreement with regard to the concept and the way of working at the SUP of Sarajevo, and my position in the ministry. So, and that was spelled out, openly. Mr. Stanisic accepted that the differences between his concept and mine were unsurmountable. Because the CSB of Sarajevo was one of the most important CSBs in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we agreed with Mr. Stanisic that he be appointed advisor in the minister's office, but his workplace remained in the building of the city secretariat, and he never moved physically to the building of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us something about the barricades yesterday. Let's see if we can deal with this quite shortly and look at some of the documents that relate to it. How did you find out, please, very briefly, sir, that these barricades had been arrested [sic] on the 1st of March?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko Dukic called me on the phone and informed me that there had been a murder by the church in Sarajevo and, for that reason, barricades had been set up in Sarajevo, and that the SDS was behind that, as a response to that act, which had been committed at a wedding. As far as I remember, that was around 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause there for a moment because page 51, line 9, it says barricades had been "arrested." Erected is what I said. All right. So you were told by Rajko Dukic that the barricades gone up in response to this killing, the SDS was behind it. What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the building. Meanwhile, I already had problems at some barricades. I was stopped because representatives of the SDS were saying that I wasn't the person to continue making decisions, because the Assembly of the SDS had, allegedly, appointed Mr. Stanisic the Serb minister. And I apologise, if I'm using the wrong term now. But I was able to reach the building eventually. I walked around some barricades, and then I tried to contact the members of the Presidency and the political leaders. Mr. Dukic said to me that Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik were in Belgrade at an important meeting. Later, I found out that they were gambling with Arkan at the Yugoslavia Hotel. I tried to contact the other members of the Presidency and was able to speak to Mr. Izetbegovic, who showed no interest whatsoever to find a solution to the issue of the barricades. He said that it was for the MUP to take care of that. Meanwhile, I had called my co-workers to come to headquarters urgently and see what we could do to avoid conflict because the SDA had already started erecting barricades too. And my assistants responded to my call. They came to headquarters. We were in my office all the time, setting up contact with the local police stations to be fully informed what this was all about and why barricades had been set up. Also, because the active police force should try to prevent an escalation of violence at certain spots, and we also wanted to prevent clashes between opposing barricades. I mean, Serb and Muslim barricades. And I cannot say whether it was on that day or on the following day that I decided to call up a part of the reserve police in Sarajevo. And around 1.00 or 2.00 a.m., I was able to speak to Ms. Plavsic. She responded, and she was surprised, she didn't know about the barricades. She said to me that she would come to my office so that we may see what we could do. And I informed her that I already spoken to Mr. Izetbegovic and -- who answered that he wanted to -- to get a good night's sleep rather than take care of problems that the MUP should take care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I wanted as many people from the MUP to come, so that we could take care of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please. Because we looked earlier yesterday about the conversation about Mr. Plavsic which -- Mr. Dukic. Before we look at a couple of other conversations, I want do show you, please, a short clip from the Death of Yugoslavia about the barricades. I have no idea what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: THE NARRATOR: "For centuries Muslims, Serbs, and Croats have lived here together. Now they had to choose a future. Half the Yugoslav republics had gone for independence, and it was time for the Bosnians to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] we created a situation in which" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] but the Muslims and Croats wanted it out. I was clear that Bosnia was doomed." THE NARRATOR: "Muslims and Croats were the majority, so the president won his vote. He was expecting trouble, but he didn't know it would start from his own side. It happened as the guests arrived at a Serb wedding. The Muslim killed the father of the groom. That night, Serbs hit back. Their gunmen erected armed barricades all over the Bosnian capital."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The Serbs of Sarajevo demand, number one" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just pause for a moment there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was that speaker?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Rajko Dukic. Mr. Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] That the Bosnian government stopped seeking international recognition of the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina." THE NARRATOR: "Neither the Bosnian police nor the Green Berets and Muslim paramilitaries under Izetbegovic were strong enough to take own the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Then we decided" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That's all we need.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see the scene that we saw of the police officer -- sorry, of a person at the barricades pointing a gun, was that a seen that you saw when you were doing your tour of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a normal, scene. I visited all barricades, and at some I was arrested, simply because I had decided not to use the police, either active or reserve units, to scatter the barricades, but I wanted to resolve the issue with political means. So I went from one barricade to another all night through, and on the following day, because I wanted to calm down the situation and prevent open conflict. As you saw from these videos they were armed persons at these barricades so that Sarajevo was completely blocked, and they controlled the passing of the civilian population. And then the -- that's -- that's why I wanted the Presidency to make a decision about the solution to the barricades issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if that clip could be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P907.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so we can deal with film clips at the same time, I want to you have a look at a short clip from the film -- the documentary Serbian Epics, which is 65 ter 2931.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Mico Stanisic. I apologise, Your Honour, my emotion -- my reaction is a bit emotional. I believe that you will appreciate how I feel watching the footage which confirmed that my country is dying, and I apologise for my emotional reaction. Could I please be given a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are a few minutes short of the ordinary break, so we would rise at this time and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, I trust you have sufficiently recovered in order to continue your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask to you look at a bit more of there film.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will take a lot more to recover from everything, but there you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we just pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Until the time of your resignation at the beginning of April, did you ever see Stanisic wearing uniform like that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nor did I have an occasion to meet with Stanisic after I resigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just play the rest then, please. I just want to ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I'm Mico Stanisic, interior minister of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here you see my closest collaborators, participants in the first battle for our Serbian people, and they're also participants in the first victory" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we need translation, it's subtitled, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause, please, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Karisik, had he been appointed as head of the Special Police by the time you had resigned?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Karisik was Dragan Bikic's deputy in the special unit while I was there. And later on, as I can see, he was appointed the commander of the special unit when Mr. Stanisic took over the role as the minister in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next person that he is about to identify, we can see the name on the screen, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatko Brdar, yes, I knew him, he was also a special unit member. I wasn't aware of the fact that he had a command role.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just play to the end of this, and then we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mane -- I'm not sure that I know the person. But looking at him, I would say that is also a former member of the Special Police unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I wanted to play.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, although I played it in opening, it actually hasn't been admitted yet. Could that be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have just the date of this video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: June 1992, and I'm sorry, I can't remember the exact date. But it is June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P908, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We know, Dr. Zepinic, and I have got a number of other things to cover with you that the barricades incident was in fact settled by a form of negotiation. But I want to ask you to you look at some intercepts, please, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner, again, I believe you offered this as -- as document to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I asked for it to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have up, please, very, very quickly a couple of the conversations that took place during the barricades. The first is in tab 31, for the interpreters. It is 1052.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And because of the time I'm not going to do too much of the contents. But you listened to this, and we can see that Mrs. Plavsic is saying, in the middle of the first page, that the minister is here, the deputy minister, Mr. Jusuf, is here, as far as the MUP. Were you there -- is this when she was there with you or you were there with them, or is this somebody else?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there. The meeting was held in the morning on the 2nd of March, 1992, around 8.00 in the morning in the Presidency building. Delimustafic and I were there, I don't know who this Jusuf is. Whether it was Jusuf Pusina or whether it was Jusuf who was Mr. Abdic's head of office. I can't identify the person. But, yes, the two of us were there, and discussed the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you listened to the tape, were you able to the voices of Plavsic, Dukic, Ostojic, and Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, then he was present for this one, so may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P909, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to you look, however, please, at a conversation with -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is tab 36, please, 1427. And it's the 2nd of March, during the incident again. Now, when you listened to this, were you able to identify the voices of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Dukic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I identified their voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In the middle of the first page, Mr. Stanisic says when he's asked, Where you are calling from? I am up there, at Vrace's community hall. Were you aware that that's where he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then if we go, please, to the third page in English, and the second page in the B/C/S. Stanisic is saying to Mr. Dukic, Since was visited there, I visited all the check-points. He says, Sarajevo is ours, 100 percent. And he repeats that. Did you ever see him? You were visiting the various barricades or whatever, did you ever see him during any of this?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have an occasion to see Mr. Stanisic at any of the barricades, and I find this statement of his surprising, given the fact that the SDA also erected barricades. So it is really surprising for me to hear that he could tour and inspect all the barricades because he would have had to pass through the SDA barricade in order to reach the SDS barricades. But during that night or the following morning, I did not see him on any of the barricades, be it those erected by the SDA or those erected by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, then this is one should be simply marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P910, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I want to ask you about the conversations on the barricades. Can we just look briefly, please, at a report that was prepared after the incident, and that is 376, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 376? I hope we're connected to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] See if we can put up the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, we seem to have e-court problems again, so we will see if we can put this document up in Sanction. Yeah. And if we could have the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a long report, Dr. Zepinic, so I just want you to -- was a report done by the -- by someone - it is dated, but it doesn't look like it is signed at the end - on the barricades incidents, and were you made aware of this report?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the report. I have not seen it before I started today in the courtroom. When I read it, I believe that the report is not complete. This is probably just one part or some of the information obtained by the State Security Service, but there was other information held by crime services and public security services about the participation of persons on the barricades and the incident that took place there. And, obviously, all the consequences which took place two days thereafter, when the perpetrator was brought in but then released without any charges being brought against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I -- because it is a long report, I haven't got time to go through it. When you read it, the contents of the report, did that seem to be accurate to you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially accurate but not fully accurate. I would say that it is not fully accurate. It doesn't provide the full information about the complete security situation with regard to the incidents that took place in Sarajevo between the 1st and the 4th of March. I would not accept this report as an official report on behalf of the Ministry of the Interior with regard to the incidents on the barricades because it does not contain all the elements that the ministry was privy to as obtained based on the intelligence, the circumstances of the murder, the participation of various persons in manning the barricades, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to ask that it be admitted as an exhibit -- Your Honour, it is going -- just can I finish. It is going take me too long to take him through all the bits to say which is accurate and which is inaccurate. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I hear from Mr. Zecevic, Ms. Korner I'm at lot as to the basis of this. You're seeking the exhibit through this witness. A, he hasn't seen it before; B, from what he has seen he has grave reservations, to put it mildly, about the accuracy of what it contains; C, it's incomplete. So the -- I can understand your having it marked for identification, but I really don't see it admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well, then, Your Honour. I will have it marked for identification. That is fine for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm thankful to Your Honour. There is nothing more I can add to you analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P911, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, very quickly, can we have up -- in fact what is a -- already a Defence exhibit, I'm told, 1D120?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Before we go on, I see the transcript reads --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, the transcript at line -- page 63, line 23, my comments on Ms. Korner's application from what he has seen, he has grave reservation to "future mindly" about the accuracy about what it contains. What I did say is, "to put it mildly."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One always hopes these things will be corrected when it's listened to in the background, but I agree it is probably better to be safe than sorry. Can we have 1D120 up, please. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the -- the council for the protection of the constitutional order. And if we go to the second page in each, we can see your name as an attendee. Is that right, you did attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I attended those sessions almost regularly and Professor Plavsic was the chairperson of that council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that. Now in fact you told us earlier you thought Mr. Stanisic had been -- or you had been told at the barricades that he been appointed minister of the interior at the beginning of the March. In fact, he was - we know because we have documents - he was appointed on the 23rd of -- 24th of March, I'm sorry. Between this period in March and your resignation on the 4th of April, can I deal with this quite shortly, did you in fact receive information that Arkan and his forces were in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was put in charge by the Presidency, together with Mr. Fikret Abdic, who was a member of the Presidency; Mr. Simovic; and Mr. Jerko. Delimustafic and I, actually, were put in charge of going to Bijeljina and dealing with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to take that shortly, as I say, because I want to come on to the circumstances of your resignation and arrest. Was the upshot there that you were told when were stopped by a check-point - and I am leading on this, and I hope there is no dispute - and you were then told that Mico Stanisic had been appointed as minister of the interior, Serbian minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the interview on TV and problems with avoiding the assassination, we managed to get to the airport. A helicopter took us to Tuzla from the barracks there, we were transferred to the centre of security, and then a volunteer took us to Bijeljina, and our column was stopped on the road by a group led by an SDS MP, Kerovic. I can't remember his name. He asked me to step out of the vehicle because they wanted to kill me, because I no longer represented anybody and had no authority in the Ministry of the Interior from the positions of the SDA -- SDS, which, according to him, had, in the meantime, appointed Mico Stanisic for the Serbian minister in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Had you been informed -- a simple yes or no, had you been informed in advance that Mr. Stanisic was going to be appointed?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, to be honest with you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can you look, please, very quickly at a document dated the 1st of April, which is -- actually, it seems to have been exhibited already apparently. I can't read what that is. 1D78? Let's hope it's the right one. I didn't -- no. No, it is not. Could I have up, please, 65 ter 2768.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's 1D78, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, it is an error, and it should be 2 -- 65 ter 2768.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. No, that's wrong. All right. Oh, no it is. It is the right document, I beg your pardon. Can we just look at the second paragraph -- not -- on the English. Don't worry about the B/C/S. I think it is the first paragraph in the B/C/S. It says the following members of the current advisory board of the MUP discussed this matter about the organisation for internal affairs, et cetera, on the 1st of April, and it shows you. Is that right, did you discuss this matter? Did you have a discussion on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. However, I know that I invited to my office my assistants, including Mr. Stanisic, I wanted to discuss the complete situation. But I'm not sure that that was on the 1st of April, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is apparently -- it's an official document, it looks like. And it talks about this meeting on the 1st of April, and then we better look at the second page, please, in English, and still on that page in B/C/S. Having realistically reviewed the evidence situation, et cetera et cetera, the advisory board decided the existing MUP should be transformed peacefully and without excesses. Do you remember attending a meeting where this was discussed. And please just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show the signature on this document to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's -- it says Kolegij MUP.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot refrain from commenting this document, which is the worst garbage. Because this signature, the collegium of the MUP, means nothing at all. A dispatch can be sent on behalf of the MUP by the minister, his deputy, or his assistants for some -- for some division. But I don't know who may have represented the collegium of the MUP and had the authority to send out such a dispatch, especially since it was addressed to some federal institutions. But to come back to the meeting you mentioned, it is true that I invited my co-workers to my office. It was not a collegium meeting but an initiative of mine to say good bye to each other. And I said then -- Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can. Can I just say, I'm just being reminded how little time there is, so if you can keep it short. All right. Before this meeting had you become aware of Mandic's telegram about the MUP -- the split in the MUP and Mr. Delimustafic's response?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date when I got acquainted with the dispatch that Mr. Mandic sent on behalf of the CSB, and without any authority to do so, but I know that there was an initiative for the two of us to co-sign a dispatch and send it out to all organs and the services of the MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which we would invite all staff to continue carrying out their duties in accordance with the law and regulations. I believe that it was sometime in April, but at that time I spent more time in a -- or on a helicopter, than in my -- in a bed. I went to Bijeljina, visited special units, went to Bratunac. I was in the field much more than in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you, please, the response which you collaborated with on with Mr. Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1D136, is that right? It has been -- it has definitely been exhibited, in which case I'm not going to bother.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But can I show you, please, the Mandic dispatch. Sorry forget that, I don't have time. All right. 1st of April, this -- on the 4th of April, did you have a meeting with the special forces -- sorry, on the 3rd of April, with the commander, Mr. Vikic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only with Vikic but also other commanders who came to see me on the evening when I returned from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Karisik attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, please, in two sentences, what was the purpose of this meeting? What did you want to do?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was for the minister and me to appear together before all the units of the Special Police and the commanding staff and point out that it was necessary that the service function as a single service and that they support -- they enjoyed our support in doing so, because the circumstances had grown out of control. But when it comes to the unity of the -- these units, we emphasised that and that they should act in accordance with the law and legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your view, Dr. Zepinic, what was going to be the effect of splitting the MUP in the fashion that it happened?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I start with the special unit. With regard to the circumstances and the crises that were popping up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the special unit received orders to be in full combat readiness. And you can imagine 3 to 400 young men fully armed and in full combat gear trained to carry out the most complex police interventions what it would have meant if any kind of incident had occurred within the unit. Probably we would have witnessed such a massacre within the unit, and the consequences would have been disastrous. And this opinion applies to the entire MUP. A division of the MUP and its staff that were appointed on ethnic grounds. And the ensuing establishment of MUPs, ethnically-based MUPs in one country, in which a ministry -- ministry staff should be mono-ethnic, a consequence of all that would have been a -- an armed conflict, and we all know what eventually came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Can we look first, please, at your resignation letter, and then if could you tell the Court how you came to resign.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, 1786.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my resignation, addressed to Mr. Krajisnik as the Speaker of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the president of the Assembly of the SDS. It was drafted during the meeting. I received a phone call while we had a meeting with the special unit from Mr. Krajisnik in person, ordering me to -- to stop the meeting and come immediately to the assembly, and I replied that - I called the meeting; it was my initiative - and that we'll have the meeting and after which I will come to his office, and he accepted that. I did so. And, upon coming there, in the waiting-room in front of his office there was some armed and masked individuals whom I didn't know in full combat gear so that my escort and my driver were a bit frightened by that. And the entire leadership of the SDS was in Krajisnik's office. Karadzic was there. Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Djeric, Mr. Stanisic, and others. And I also noticed, among others, that there was Momcilo Mandic present. I also saw Karisik there, and I immediately asked him why he hadn't attended the meeting that I had called the previous night for all commanders, and why he didn't come to the meeting at the special unit, because he was still the Deputy Commander of that unit. Mr. Stanisic reacted to that very angrily by saying that I was undermining the concept, the -- on which the parties had agreed about the splitting of the MUP and the splitting of the special unit. My reaction was that if such a meeting had taken place, it would have been natural for me to be informed about it. The atmosphere was very tense. Mr. Stanisic, even produced a pistol to shoot at me, and then I said, Well, let's at least go down to the basement and not do in the office of the Speaker of the Assembly. Mr. Krajisnik was the only person there trying to calm down the situation. Dr. Karadzic, and especially the late Dr. Koljevic were extremely aggressive with regard to my opposition of the concept of ethnically-based parties. He stated -- or, rather, repeated the type of statements that he had uttered often, and I, again, offered my resignation to Mr. Krajisnik as the Speaker of the assembly to Mr. Pelivan who was the prime minister and Mr. Izetbegovic who was the president of the Presidency, and that they should have accepted rather than refused my resignation. Mr. Karadzic commented that it was easier to replace Tito than me and such nonsense. The atmosphere was very tense. And there were many weapons there. My driver and me only had light arms, our personal weapons, which was usual, side-arms, and Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Stanisic, I'm not sure, said that the Serb members of the special unit were unwilling to leave or take any instructions from anybody expect me. I reacted by saying that I would resign if -- if I personally was a hindrance to the implementation of the policy of ethnically-based parties, which Mr. Krajisnik accepted. In the meantime, Mr. Simovic had left and brought this document which I signed, and I didn't even look what it said. I wasn't interested. It was very clear that it would be inevitable -- or, rather, that our division or rift would be inevitable. There was a -- an argument about my opposition to the splitting of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP and about my opinion that in case this should happen, the consequences would be disastrous for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Krajisnik was calming the situation. This went on for an hour or two, and -- until they said to me that in the hallway there were two or three -- I know Mr. Repja and Mr. Maric who were commanders in the special unit of the police, and there is one more person whose name I can't recall now, they were armed in full combat gear with hand grenades, automatic rifles, pistols, knives, so there was a great likelihood that conflict could break out among them three. And in the office of Mr. Krajisnik there were some armed persons wearing paramilitary uniforms. I asked Mr. Repja and Mr. Maric to sit down. There was no need to intervene, which Mr. Repja had wanted to do. Probably from preventing us from killing each other. And then we went to the office across the floor from the -- from the one in which we were, and then I believe Mr. Stanisic, Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, were with me, and I can't remember who else still was. I believe it was Momcilo Mandic and Karisik. At that moment, Repja issued an order - I would call it that. He took his automatic weapon into his hands, and he ordered everybody else to leave because he wanted to speak to his supervisor. And he said that he wouldn't listen to any -- anybody else's orders but to mine. I stayed there with only the three of them in that room. I explained that I had resigned, that the situation was what it was, and that I actually had no more authority or accountability now. So I couldn't demand them do anything, but I requested them to show understanding. I had known many of them from earlier times, especially Repja, he was a member of the same karate club as me. And Maric was one of my students, so they were totally loyal. Some of them asked me later why I hadn't told them to arrest or kill some of the people in Mr. Krajisnik's office, but I never had that idea. It was far for me to do that. After that, Repja went to the office next door and ordered Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic, and the others to return to the room in which I was. Then he produced his official ID. He tore it up and said, This is the only man I will obey. And he left the room. The atmosphere -- well, you can imagine what it was like. I requested to be -- requested them to let me go, to return to my family because I had no more official position. I was merely a citizen like everybody else. But then Mr. Krajisnik and the others again entreated me to give it a second thought and join them in -- in keeping up political functioning, but I replied, I took no interest in that. I left the building. I sat in my car. I am not sure what happened to my escort because there was just a driver waiting for me. The escort probably left with Repja. My driver burst out in tears, and he said to -- that he had been ordered by Mr. Momcilo Mandic to kill me. Otherwise, they would kill my family. My driver who had driven me for a long time told me, Minister, I cannot kill you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, Zoran, think of your family. Anyway, we reached my apartment. When I entered my apartment, the special forces who were my body-guards, I informed them that they were no longer obliged to mind me and that they could leave, but they refused my request and said that they would stand by me and mind me as long as they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, just one thing I want to ask you about. You say Stanisic pulled out a gun and waved it at you, and you said, ready to go down to the basement. When he pulled out the gun, did he say anything as to why he was waving the gun at you?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot faithfully reflect his words. But he said that there was no other way to have it out with me other than kill me, because I opposed the concept embraced by the ethnic parties. Other methods proved unsuccessful, and the assassinations that were organised were also unsuccessful. And I would now once again like to thank all those who saved me. And Stanisic said, Well, we can't come to terms with this guy in other way, so let's kill him to prevent him from causing us any further headache. But he may have -- he may be able to come up with another reason later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you went home. And when you -- after you -- you went home, did you -- were you in your apartment the following day. And did you hear gun-shot from the direction of Vrace?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Upon returning home, I didn't go to the MUP on the following day. And I stayed in my apartment, which is actually a little studio in Lenin Street, number 52, on the tenth floor. My family was also there, all of them. And around about 3.00 -- and let me mention that the lads who were my security detail from the special unit. I heard over the radio that the attack on Vrace had started around about 3.00 on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Over the police communication system, who did you hear in connection with this attack?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listening to police radio communication, I recognised the voices of Mr. Mandic; Mr. Stanisic; Mr. Mladjen Mandic, Momo Mandic's brother; and the voice of Jusuf Pusina. I believe that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what they doing, Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic, in particular? What were they saying?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now what the conversation was exactly like. But I remember well that Mladjen Mandic, Momo's brother, said come on, Momo, let's get this over with, because there were students who were lying on the ground on a football pitch between the two sides, not to detail I remember, but I cannot paraphrase the conversation between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Pusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, between then and 18th of July, did you remain in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And on the --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my entire family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you decide that the only thing to do would be to leave Bosnia, and, as a result, in August, did you go to the Canadian embassy?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in Sarajevo, I was under terrible pressure, and thanks, first of all, to some colleagues and friends and thanks to those who took my kids under their protection, we remained alive. There were several instances where I was interviewed, interrogated, questioned to the effect that why I was still in Sarajevo and so on. In a previous interview, I said that if I was to be forced to leave Sarajevo, then I would leave Bosnia and Yugoslavia as well because Sarajevo is in the centre of my heart. This is the best town in the world. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do apologise -- know this is -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [in English] ... Okay, we're going back to your question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to you when you were outside the Canadian embassy?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the Canadian embassy, there were two cars in front of it. Mr. Stanisic emerged from one of the cars. He was the only person I recognised. With some four or five fully armed individuals in combat fatigues. And they forced me to enter one of the cars and to be driven with them. I said to Mr. Stanisic that I had an appointment with the -- Mr. Pavle Bulatovic - who was murdered, unfortunately. He was a great friend of mine, and we shared some ideas of unity - because I had met Mr. Bulatovic on the previous day. But Mr. Stanisic said, Just you come along with us. We have to apprehend you, and we will sort things out with Mr. Bulatovic. They tried to handcuff me. I asked Mr. Stanisic not to do so. He accepted my request, so I was not handcuffed eventually. They transferred me to another vehicle. There were two escorts, Mr. Stanisic and an escort in -- and a driver in one vehicle. In the other vehicle I was placed between two armed individuals who were holding their side-arms at the ready, and there was another person in the passenger seat in combat fatigues, and the driver was also armed and also wearing combat fatigues. I was taken to Vila Bosanska, where I encountered Dr. Koljevic who was emerging from Vila Bosanska. He uttered very nasty comments to the effect, Oh, we finally caught you. He demanded of Mr. Stanisic for me to be urgently transferred to Pale to prison and he insisted with Mr. Stanisic that I be handcuffed. Mr. Stanisic refused that. I would like to thank Mr. Stanisic for that. Later on, they bundled me into that car as well and then the two cars set out towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop for the moment. Sorry to interrupt, but where is the Vila Bosanska?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry, I should explain that. [Interpretation] Vila Bosanska is an edifice building -- well, in former Yugoslavia there were buildings which were residencies of Republican delegations whenever federal organs had sessions. There was Slovenian villa, Bosnian villa, et cetera. And this was used by the Bosnian delegation. And when it's war broke out, the SDS took over that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is the building in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. So that the car that arrested you in Sarajevo took you to Belgrade did it? Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, sorry. A mistake. [In English] I was arrested in Belgrade in front of Canadian embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Belgrade, right. And the car that took you first to the Vila Bosanska and then where to?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two vehicles. In the front vehicle, Mr. Stanisic, his escorts in that vehicle. I was in the second vehicle. After a brief stay at -- or in front of Vila Bosanska, we did not enter the building. We were in the parking lot. But after Dr. Koljevic emerged from that building, it was decided that they should transfer me to Pale. I cannot recall whether Dr. Koljevic mentioned Dr. Karadzic, but it was known to me that Dr. Karadzic supposedly wanted to see me there, so they bundled me into the same car and the same two armed individuals with an escort in the passengers seat and the driver, who was also armed, and we set out towards Pale from that point -- from that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to, I'm afraid, cut this slightly short. But in order to go to Pale you had to pass through, obviously, the Serbian border and check-points. Did any -- was any attempt made to stop the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At no check-points, be it in Serbia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina. From Belgrade to the Bosnian-Serbian border, we passed a number of check-points. Obviously the number plates, or the car of Mr. Stanisic were known to the personnel manning those check-points. There were they were not checked. We had no -- our IDs checked. When we crossed the border and entered Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were not stopped at any check-points until we reached Pale, which means we were not stopped at any check-points, and we were not controlled or searched at any of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to deal with your imprisonment were you, first of all, kept in a villa in -- in Pale, in -- on Mount Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After reaching Pale, first, we briefly stayed at a facility intended for the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, where Mr. Stanisic had offices. I was offered a sandwich there. After a brief stay there, I was transferred to the Vucko facility, a facility that had been built for the Sarajevo Olympics. I was the only detainee in that building. There were 20 armed individuals for no apparent reason, or no reason apparent to me, who were allegedly guarding me. I had terrible health problems at the time. There were no other detainees in that building. I was on my own. Unfortunately, they did not have water supply nor electricity, but you know the conditions were as they were, and that facility is on Mount Jahorina, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you have exceeded your extended time by more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am aware of that, Your Honour, but it is really important. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How much longer do you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to deal with two other matters, his transfer from various prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And how long do you expect that would take?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Depends on the witness, rather, but I hope that we can keep it quite short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Because the adjournment time is 15 minutes away, and there are two brief matters which the Court would like to address in the last five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Perhaps if I can lead on this, it may be quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Zepinic, I'm sorry you have had to be cut short on what was obviously an appalling time for you. But, first of all, can you look at a document, very quickly, which is an order putting you in custody. I'm sorry I've lost the -- 1969, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, and could I tender the previous document whatever the number was, as an exhibit. His resignation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P912.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is apparently a decision of the 2nd of September, 1992, and can we see the bottom, please, in both documents. It's got a signature. Are you able to recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose signature this is. I think that Mico Stanisic is supposed to be cited here. But who signed this and whether this is his signature, I cannot say. The decision on detention was handed over to me. I said them, How could you expect of me to appeal to a superior Court within in 24 hours in Sarajevo while I was being detained here in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And what I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, before we go on, I just note that the transcript at line 1 on page 79 records me as saying, "Yes, chick, chick." I have no idea what that is supposed to mean. Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The reason given from your arrest is that you recruited citizens of Serbian nationality to serve in military formations of the enemy. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know who the enemy was in this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think -- I think the idea is that you recruited people to fight in the Croat or the Muslim formations. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This accusation is the stupidest thing that could be attributed to me that I was mobilising people for any formation units of any ethnic background, and least of all for the purposes of the enemy. I never saw members of any other ethnic group as enemies. I've never categorised people on the basis of their ethnicity, religion, or the number of -- or the colour of their skin, neither will I do so any -- any time. I, first of all, refuse for this term "enemy" to be used in such communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you then transferred --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. May that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P913.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you transferred from this vila then to Lukavica prison -- to Kula prison in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after a couple of days of investigation and mistreatment in the Vucko facility, I was transferred to prison of Lukavica -- Lukavica civilian prison. I spent some time there. And after that I was transferred to the army barracks at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you in fact in custody between September 1992 to late November 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, 80, line 23, I don't think the witness says "army barracks." I believe he said something different. So if my colleague can check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right, Dr. Zepinic? First of all, you were in the civilian prison --

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was prison at Lukavica, and after that I was -- civilian, after that I was transferred to the military prison within the army barracks at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And eventually, effectively, did you escape? I think you were allowed out and then made your escape.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My escape from detention was, so to speak, aided on the part of some individuals who were in the area. Yes, I did escape with the help of friends. I did not organise the breakout.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, due to the intervention of Mr. Zecevic, the witness failed to answer the question about how long he was detained from September to November. Could he answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right - thank you, Your Honour. Dr. Zepinic, I put the dates to you. Is that about right, Dr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was the end of November, beginning of December, when I managed to escape from Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The Court has been told of an occasion during the assembly when Milan Trbovic suggested to the assembly that you had become, an assembly in November, the 23rd and 24th, that you became an officer of the military security. Did you ever become an officer in military security?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never become an officer in military security, neither did I have any posts in the military. I have heard such statements that I was a general, a colonel, you name it. This was mere claptrap, on the part of Mr. Trbovic. I don't know where he got that idea from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, on the topic of your imprisonment and all together you made statements to the Serbian police during the course of your incarceration. How were you treated, if can you do that very briefly, during this incarceration?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to say, and I would like to mention the name of Tomo Puhalac whom I known and who was a member of the State Security Service while I was in power who was quite fair and conducts himself as per regulations. As far as the conducts of other members, well, their conduct should be the matter for their conscience, and I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What I'm asking is whether when you made those statements, you did so voluntarily and without any threats or inducements.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably none of us who were incarcerated was free of pressure or threats. I believe that Mr. Karadzic, while was in the military prison in Lukavica, came and asked me where my family was. During the investigation my interrogators insisted on learning where the rest of my family was. On this occasion, can I thank my mentor, friend, and Professor Sternic of the -- professor of a medical faculty in Sarajevo who -- in Belgrade who protected my family and hid them away from those who wanted to detect their whereabouts. I must emphasise that other people had it worse during incarceration than I had. But the only person who was professional in his conducts with Mr. Tomo Puhalac, and he was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Zepinic. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, the next thing to happen would be your cross-examination by counsel in turn for each of the accused. That will not happen today. As I indicated, you -- your testimony will continue on Monday, and I will -- something I failed to do yesterday which I will do now, and that is to caution you that having been sworn as a witness you cannot have any contact with the lawyers from either side. And in such conversations as you may have with persons outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So the Court will not rise immediately, because it has certain procedural matters with which to deal. But you are now excused as a witness, to return to this courtroom -- sorry, where are we on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To return -- you will be escorted to Courtroom I for 9.00 on Monday morning. So we trust that you have a safe weekend. And you are now excused. The usher will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber will now give an oral ruling in respect of a matter which the written reasons and the full decision will follow shortly. The Trial Chamber will now rule on the Prosecution's motion to amend the mode of testimony of Witness ST-140, ST-150 and ST-176, and to re-instate Witness ST-74 filed on the 10th of December, 2009, in so far as it concerns Witness ST-150. Since the witness is scheduled to testify on Tuesday the 2nd of February, in its motion the Prosecution request that witness ST-150 be permitted to testify pursuant to the provision of Rule 92 ter instead of viva voce. The Chamber is not satisfied that this request is in the interests of justice and, therefore, denies the motion in this respect requiring that witness, ST-150 testify viva voce. The Prosecution may use up to three hours to conduct its examination-in-chief. As I said the full written reasons will follow in respect of the motion of which the Chamber remains seized. The other matter is that yesterday the Chamber raised with counsel for the Prosecution the prospect of suspending or reserving a period in order to deal with the outstanding matter of adjudicated facts. The Chamber, considering the -- what Ms. Korner had to say yesterday about her schedule of witnesses for the week of the 8th of February, nevertheless, has determined that it is during the week of the 8th of February that it will suspend the hearings in Court so that they it can dispose of this matter. So counsel would therefore make the -- consequential arrangements accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that. It may cause difficulties, but for the moment I will say nothing else. Is it Your Honours intention also to deal finally with the other motions as well in this week? Can I just ask that? Because we have been told repeatedly that it will be dealt with. And we are in the process of filing further motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber, of course, is not unmindful of the outstanding motions. So the answer -- the only answer that I could sensibly make to your question is that it is intended that priority is given to disposing of these adjudicated facts because -- the motion in respect of adjudicated facts, because clearly a number of other matters are contingent upon the decision in that respect, and the other motions will, of course, be dealt with accordingly. So we take the adjournment, to resume, as I said in this -- sorry, in Courtroom I, at 9.00, on Monday morning. And I wish everyone a safe weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
